Q: How to display menu bar icons with GTK 4? A:

GTK 4 does not provide a clean public API to force menu icons globally. Instead of walking the internal widget tree, using custom menu children for items that need icons is safer and more future-proof.

Q: Cannot call "na" with argument "x"="call "operator !=" (series bool)" A:

In v6, scripts must explicitly cast a numeric value to “bool” to use it where a “bool” type is required.

Q: How to hide an API key in SvelteKit so it's not visible in the browser? A:

Server-only modules:

Like a good friend, SvelteKit keeps your secrets. When writing your backend and frontend in the same repository, it can be easy to accidentally import sensitive data into your front-end code (environment variables containing API keys, for example). SvelteKit provides a way to prevent this entirely: server-only modules.

  1. Use your (hardcoded) API key in an internal +server API endpoint.
  2. Call your internal API endpoint from +page.svelte
  3. Optional: instead of hardcoding, put your API key in a private env variable. Now your API key will not be in your git commit history and Svelte will warn you if you accidentally use it from a browser-visible file.

Q: Creating an non constructible object: issue with trivially copyable definition? A:

such behavior [creating an object of a non-constructible class] is undesirable as it violates the class semantic.

I see a different semantic than you. Yes, all of the constructors are deleted, but there are several non-static member functions that are not deleted. These member functions cannot be called unless an object of this type exists, so why would they be explicitly defined unless they could be called? I infer from the existence of these functions that there is an intent that somehow objects of this non-constructible class could exist. While there might not have been such an intent, the behavior you discovered supports this conclusion.

If you change each default to delete, then I would agree that the semantic is that no objects of this class should exist. Of course, if you do that, then the bit_cast line will not compile... Fix the semantics, and the issue disappears.

Note: The destructor is a key aspect of the above. If no destructor had been declared, I would have included "add ~Test() = delete;" among the changes to make to get the desired semantic.

the non-constructible class can be a base implementation class that must be used only as inherited

This could be made clearer in the code. How is this semantic conveyed to someone reading this code? By the protected status of the BaseImpl(int) constructor? As you make a class definition larger, it becomes harder for the reader to account for every constructor. That is, relying on constructors to convey that a class must be used only as a base class is unreliable (also fragile, since it is easy to add a new constructor in the public section). A better way to convey this semantic is to make the destructor protected.

  • See also C++ Core Guideline C.35: "A base class destructor should be either public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual" (not to be confused with the similar C.127, which would apply only if there was a virtual function). Admittedly, private inheritance does mitigate the risk of not following this guideline, but it is still useful advice.

A protected destructor would prevent the bit_cast method, unless you are compiling with MSVC, which is non-conforming in this respect. Again, a clearer semantic makes the issue disappear.

Also, you should not call a class "non-constructible" when it has a usable constructor. Constructing an instance of a class as a sub-object counts as constructing an instance of the class.

Q: Where to place window.addEventListener('online' A:

FYI there is a new API import { on } from 'svelte/events'

[In order to avoid gotchas with Svelte's event delegation] it's better to use the on function imported from svelte/events rather than addEventListener, as it will ensure that order is preserved and stopPropagation is handled correctly.

The online/offline events don't seem to be delegated, so it probably won't matter for those events. I would handle these events in the root +layout.svelte onMount().

Q: Python OpenCV set timeout on VideoCapture A:

When opening the stream you only get a video object. Then you have to start reading the frames from the video object. This will tell you if there is a video stream.

TIMEOUT: The code stops if during 10 seconds no frames have been received.

RESET TIMEOUT: If within the 10 seconds new frames are being received then receiving resumes and the timeout will be again 10 seconds.

I have tested this code on a video file. I think it should work on your camera also.

import cv2
import time

try:
    cap = cv2.VideoCapture("rtsp://Username:Password@IP_ADDRESS:PORT")
    print("Stream found.")

    stream_ok = True
    while True:
        try:
            success, video_frame = cap.read()
            if success:
                print('Frame read')
                frame_ok = True
                # show frame
                cv2.imshow("Image", video_frame)
                cv2.waitKey(1)
            else:
                print('No frame read')
                frame_ok = False
        except cv2.error as e:
            print(f'CV2 Exception: {str(e)}')
            frame_ok = False

        if stream_ok:
            if not frame_ok:
                # start of missing video
                stream_ok = False
                no_frame_start_time = time.time()
        else:
            if not frame_ok:
                # still no video
                if time.time() - no_frame_start_time > 10:
                    print('NO VIDEO - CAPTURE ABORTED')
                    break
            else:
                # video restarted
                stream_ok = True

    cap.release()
    cv2.destroyAllWindows()

except:
    # It actually never reaches the exception
    print("Stream not found.")
